20 A spring of original length 100 mm is compressed by a force. The graph shows the variation of the
compressing force F with the length L of the spring.

What is the energy stored in the spring when the length is 70 mm?
A
0.090 J
B
0.21 J

hints: Notice the x-axis is length $L$ in $\text{mm}$, not compression - at $L = 70\text{ mm}$ the graph shows $F = 6\text{ N}$ and at $L = 100\text{ mm}$ $F = 0$.
Recall stored elastic energy equals work done to compress, which is the area under the $F$ against compression graph, so use the strip between $100\text{ mm}$ and $70\text{ mm}$.
Convert the compression $100 - 70 = 30\text{ mm}$ to $0.030\text{ m}$ and calculate the triangular area with base $0.030\text{ m}$ and height $6\text{ N}$.
walkthrough: Original length is $100\text{ mm}$, so when $L = 70\text{ mm}$ the compression is $x = 100 - 70 = 30\text{ mm} = 0.030\text{ m}$.
From the $F$-$L$ graph, $F = 0$ at $L = 100\text{ mm}$ and $F = 6\text{ N}$ at $L = 70\text{ mm}$, with $F$ varying linearly.
Elastic energy stored equals work done in compression, equal to the area under $F$ versus compression, which is the area under the given $F$-$L$ curve between $100\text{ mm}$ and $70\text{ mm}$.
That area is a triangle with base $0.030\text{ m}$ and maximum force $6.0\text{ N}$, so $E = \frac{1}{2}Fx = \frac{1}{2} \times 6.0 \times 0.030$.
This gives $E = 0.090\text{ J}$ with units of $\text{N m} = \text{J}$. This is option A.

A.explanation: Area from $L = 100\text{ mm}$ to $L = 70\text{ mm}$ is $\frac{1}{2} \times 0.030\text{ m} \times 6.0\text{ N} = 0.090\text{ J}$.

B.explanation: This is about $\frac{1}{2} \times 0.070\text{ m} \times 6.0\text{ N}$, which wrongly uses the full length $70\text{ mm}$ instead of the compression $30\text{ mm}$.

C.explanation: This is $\frac{1}{2} \times 0.090\text{ m} \times 6.0\text{ N}$, which wrongly uses $90\text{ mm}$ related distance instead of the $30\text{ mm}$ compression.

D.explanation: This uses $6.0\text{ N} \times 0.105\text{ m}$ style full-force times distance, missing the $\frac{1}{2}$ factor for the triangular area under the $F$-$L$ graph.
